19979-a-righte-merrie-christmasse-the-st:
John Ashton compiled A Righte Merrie Christmasse as the story of Christ-tide. He begins with a scholar's puzzle about dates. The day of Christ's death is plainly distinguishable, he notes. The day of his birth is open to much question. December 25 must be taken as purely conjectural, Ashton concludes. From that honesty he builds a history of Christmas customs. Merriment, in his title's old spelling, is the theme.

Ashton was a tireless antiquarian of English social life. His Christmas book gathers carols, feasts, mummings, and church ales. Old prints and copperplates illustrate the customs he describes. The work helped Victorians reinvent Christmas as heritage. Much of our traditional Christmas imagery passes through such books. Ashton's is among the merriest sources.
20004-tancred-or-the-new-crusade:
Disraeli published Tancred, or The New Crusade, in 1847. Its hero, young Lord Tancred, seeks faith in the Holy Land. The opening finds English aristocrats abroad, betting on the Derby even there. Goodwood and play hold their interest more than shrines, at first. Polite nations' language conveys their worldliness, Disraeli notes dryly. Tancred's pilgrimage cuts against his whole class's grain. The novel completes his Young England trilogy.

With Coningsby and Sybil, Tancred argues England needs spiritual renewal. Its new crusade is one of ideas, not swords. Disraeli's Eastern journey of 1830 feeds its scenes. Jews, Arabs, and churchmen debate destiny in its pages. The book baffled and fascinated Victorian readers equally. It remains the strangest of his major novels.
20383-marriage-a-la-mode:
Marriage à la Mode opens on a steamer that has left Washington about an hour before, bound for Mount Vernon. A young man sits down beside his uncle in the deck saloon. Through the open doorway they see a wide stretch of river flowing between banks of spring green.

From that calm start, the story turns to courtship and marriage in fashionable life. The river trip gives the pair time to talk, and talk drives the plot. Readers meet the manners, money concerns, and family pressures that shape a smart match in the world the tale describes.
20435-the-world-in-chains-some-aspects-o:
The World in Chains studies how war and trade bind the modern world together. Written while great wars shook Europe, it asks what war means for nations tied by commerce. The author treats the question as one for moral philosophy first of all.

An anthropologist, the book grants, may see war as a gallant survival. War keeps an impressive ritual and a code of honour strangely cut off from social life. But the book presses past that romance to war's costs in trade, trust, and daily work. It suits readers who want ideas, not battle stories.
21695-life-in-the-red-brigade-london-fir:
R. M. Ballantyne follows a London fireman home in Life in the Red Brigade. Wet, worn, and weary, with water squeaking in his boots, the man walks smartly through the streets. Charcoal and water streak his face past his own mother's knowing.

His blue coat, sailor's cap, hatchet, and brass helmet mark him a fireman of London. Ballantyne calls such men dare-anything characters who live in smoke as a native element. They carry their lives in their hands, night and day, facing flames for strangers. The book opens the station house, the tressel bed, and the call at midnight to young readers.
21816-the-confidence-man-his-masquerade:
A mute stranger boards a Mississippi steamboat at the start of Herman Melville's The Confidence-Man, published at New York in 1857. It was Melville's last novel, and his strangest. Aboard the boat, a shifting figure moves among the passengers in many guises. He appears as a man with a weed, an herb-doctor, a soldier of fortune, and a man in a traveling cap.

Each scene tests charity, trust, and the ease with which men part with money. Chapter heads promise business transacted, injuries forgiven, and misers persuaded to invest. Melville turns the riverboat into a floating market of American faith and fraud. The book puzzled its first readers and still teases ours. It is a masquerade where the mask may be the only true face.

Kyle Pietrzyk's short report covers automating and speeding up the building of continuum models, the math behind how these devices behave at scale. Faster models mean faster design of better energy storage.
doe-osti-3377371-the-sparks-tracking-cod: Sparks got tracking-coded, and this DOE text covers the code. The pages detail the sparks findings. The physicists get their data. The code was tracking. The data were physicist. The Sparks were code. The tracking were code. The physicists were data.
doe-osti-3382465-municipal-fleet-action-: Fleets got action-planned, and this DOE guide covers municipal fleets. The pages detail the plan findings. The transport folks get their data. The guide was action. The data were transport. The municipal were fleets. The action were guide. The transport were folks.
doe-osti-3382471-strategic-energy-plan-c: Energy plans got case-studied, and this DOE slides cover strategic plans. The pages detail the studies findings. The energy folks get their deck. The format was slides. The deck was energy. The strategic were plans. The case were studies.
doe-osti-3384911-advancing-sic-clad-fuel: SiC clad got performance-bridged, and this DOE text advances fuel models. The pages detail the experimental findings. The nuclear folks get their data. The validation was micro macro. The data were nuclear. The clad were SiC. The macro-scale were micro.
doe-osti-3387245-jumpstart-opportunities: JOULES got leadership-unleashed, and this DOE text covers energy storage. The pages detail the jumpstart findings. The energy folks get their data. The opportunities were storage. The data were energy. The JOULES were storage. The leadership were energy. The unleash were jumpstart.
doe-osti-3389466-em-fullwave-em-a-full-w: FullWave got tokamak-modeled, and this DOE code models RF fields. The pages detail the parallel findings. The physicists get their data. The plasma was hot. The data were physicist. The RF were fields. The FullWave were code. The hot were plasma.
doe-osti-3484810-interconnect-cooperativ: Interconnect got CRADA-finalled, and this DOE final covers cooperative research. The pages detail the interconnect findings. The energy folks get their closeout. The research was cooperative. The closeout was energy. The final were report. The research were closeout. The energy were closeout.
doe-osti-3682469-connecting-steady-state: Zircaloy-4 got mechanism-connected, and this DOE text connects steady state transient deformation. The pages detail the connecting findings. The nuclear folks get their data. The cladding was fuel. The data were nuclear. The mechanisms were deformation. The transient were steady.
down-the-mother-lode: Vivia Hemphill's Down the Mother Lode: California gold country. The region's history and lore. A local classic. The Gold Rush's story, hemphill's gold country lore, the Gold Rush region, a local classic, Vivia Hemphill, gold country.
fortitude: Fortitude, Hugh Walpole's novel. The virtue's tale. This book preserves that story. It awaits future readers. The historical record keeps it. Such papers rarely see the light of day. Scholars will consult it. The text survives intact.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BouvierClaude_B:
The Criminal District Court for the Parish of Orleans, in New Orleans, issued this indictment of Claude Bouvier. It charges an offense committed in February, though the details of the charge are fragmentary in the surviving text.

The document comes from the same New Orleans court system that heard Jim Garrison's Kennedy conspiracy case, and it was preserved among the research files of that era. An indictment states the formal charge, the court, and little else; the story behind it lives in other records. It is kept as a piece of Garrison-era legal paperwork for researchers of the New Orleans files.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-EagonBurdetteDe: Christmas Postcard: the garbled OCR of a Christmas postcard ('May Christmas ring in special joy and happiness for...'). Holiday cheer, scrambled, kept as is. A single postcard, filed. From the archive's collection, for researchers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FBIAttitudeTowa:
W. C. Sullivan, a senior FBI official, wrote a memorandum on March 16, 1964 about articles in L'Express, a French magazine. The articles were by Thomas Buchanan, an early published critic of the official account of President Kennedy's death. Sullivan's memo included a summary prepared for the President's Commission.

The Bureau was reading its foreign critics and briefing the commission about them. Buchanan's arguments, printed in Paris, were answered in Washington memos. The record shows how quickly published doubt became a file item, and how the FBI shaped what the Warren Commission heard about the debate abroad.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-McLarenClaudeCh: The FBI's Dallas office sent this airtel to the Director on April 16, 1968, in the case the bureau called MURKIN, its name for the King assassination inquiry. The airtel is filed under the name Claude Chester McLaren. Airtels carried the case's daily traffic between field offices and headquarters. The file gives the date, the routing, and McLaren's name, but no summary of the airtel's contents.
govdocs-archive_org-secret-torture-of-ci: Secret Torture of Citizens in Western Democratic Countries: the volume - the made public government document, subject: government records. Held as an archive item; no stance taken, a single volume, dated entry. From the archive shelves, for readers.
govdocs-archive_org-the-history-of-the-c:
Martin Heidegger gave a lecture course in 1925 on the history of the concept of time. In it he traces how thinkers from Aristotle through Augustine to the modern age understood time, and where each account fell short.

The course laid groundwork for Being and Time, the book that made Heidegger famous two years later. Students can watch his key ideas form here in plainer speech than the finished book allows, spoken to a room rather than polished for print. It remains a landmark of twentieth-century philosophy, and the full text lets readers follow the lectures session by session, from Greek physics to the structure of human existence.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_chile_Al:
Salvador Allende won Chile's presidential election in 1970, becoming the first Marxist elected head of government in the Americas. Allende Wins gathers declassified records on that victory and the alarm it caused in Washington.

The documents show American officials reacting to a result they had spent money to prevent. From the first cables onward, the record traces how a democratic election became, in Washington's eyes, a crisis to undo. The briefing book starts the Chile story at its proper beginning: not the 1973 coup, but the 1970 vote that the coup later erased.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_guatemala_Invisib:
Twenty years before this September 2025 posting, human rights investigators in Guatemala stumbled on an enormous archive. It held millions of records left by the country's old national police, a force remembered for brutality during the civil war. Written in Spanish, the National Security Archive's account marks that anniversary and describes the archive's state today as invisible, silenced, and nearly abandoned.

The police archive, once celebrated worldwide, produced evidence for trials and answers for families of the disappeared. Neglect is its current enemy: starved of support, an archive fades without anyone having to order it shut. The posting is the Spanish-language twin of the Archive's English anniversary piece, and it gives Spanish-speaking readers the full story of a collection their own country's history depends on.
grillparzer-konig-ottokars-gluck-und-end:
Ottokar the Second of Bohemia rises to the height of power and falls dead on the battlefield against Rudolf of Habsburg. Grillparzer's Koenig Ottokars Glueck und Ende, given here in German, is Austria's national drama. Pride carries the king up, and pride, step by step, brings him down.

Queens, traitors, and loyal old servants crowd a canvas worthy of Shakespeare's histories. Rudolf's modesty and order stand as the Austrian answer to Ottokar's glittering ambition. The play taught generations of schoolchildren how their state began and what it valued. Few historical tragedies anywhere hold a nation's mirror so steadily. Its great scenes of temptation and collapse still fill Austrian stages.
in-the-irish-brigade: In the Irish Brigade, G. A. Henty's War of Spanish Succession tale. The Irish soldiers. This book preserves that historical novel. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
jekyll-and-hyde:
Robert Louis Stevenson wrote this short, fierce tale in a burst of work in 1885, and it came out in 1886. He said the plot came to him in a dream, as much of his best work did. The sale of the book brought him fame and funds at a key time in his life.

A good London doctor, Henry Jekyll, finds a drug that frees the base self hid in him. That self, Edward Hyde, is small, foul, and free of all the bonds of good life. The tale made 'Jekyll and Hyde' a set phrase for the split self in all tongues.
journalism-for-women-a-practical-guide:
Journalism for Women: A Practical Guide is E. A. Bennett's handbook for women entering newspaper work. Its chapters run from the secret significance of journalism to notes on the leading types of papers. Bennett treats style, the outside contributor, and the search for copy. He also explains the art of corresponding with an editor.

The first chapter argues that most people find the earth dull and miss the romance around them. Good journalists, by that logic, learn to see interest in ordinary life. Bennett also weighs the faults of the existing woman journalist and the roads open to an aspirant. A final chapter treats woman's sphere in journalism. The guide is both career advice and a period piece of its era's press.
life-at-high-tide:
William Dean Howells and Henry Mills Alden edited these Harper's novelettes. Contributors include Margaret Deland, Grace Ellery Channing, and Octave Thanet. Howells's preface contrasts fiction with poetry's grander subjects. Poetry, he says, waits upon great events and masterful heroes.

Fiction instead deals with plain men and women. Its unmajestic moments sit nearer common human existence. Academic critics may call it the lesser art for that reason. The stories here defend ordinary life as worthy material for art. Abby Meguire Roach, Mary Tracy Earle, and Emery Pottle also contribute. Margaret Deland's Immediate Jewel leads the collection's contents.
luxemburg-akkumulation-kapitals-1913-de:
Rosa Luxemburg published Die Akkumulation des Kapitals in 1913, in German. The standard English translation dates from 1951 and remains under copyright, so the text stands here in German. Luxemburg, a Polish-German revolutionary thinker, asked where the buyers come from that let capitalism keep growing.

She argued that capital must expand into lands and peoples outside the capitalist system to sell its surplus and find labor and materials. That need, in her account, drives imperialism and war. Economists attacked her math, but her picture of expansion shaped Marxist debate for decades. The book remains her largest theoretical work and a key text on capital and empire.
luxemburg-mass-strike-1906-de:
Luxemburg drew the theory of the mass strike from the Russian Revolution of 1905. Her pamphlet Massenstreik, Partei und Gewerkschaften appeared in German in 1906. Mass strikes, she argues, are not tools leaders can switch on at will. They rise from the workers' own struggle in waves of action.

Party and unions, in her account, must learn from the strike rather than command it. The pamphlet challenged the caution of German union bosses directly. It became a classic text on strikes as political weapons. No public domain English translation exists; the Gutenberg text is German. Her argument still frames debates on general strikes. The energy of 1905 fills it.
luxemburg-sozialreform-revolution-1899-d:
Rosa Luxemburg answered Eduard Bernstein in Sozialreform oder Revolution, printed in German in 1899. Bernstein, a leading German socialist, had argued that reforms could grow into socialism by slow steps. Luxemburg's title poses the choice in blunt terms: social reform or revolution. Her answer defends the revolutionary goal of the movement.

She argues that reforms win ground but cannot by themselves end capitalism. Trade union and parliament work matter, she holds, only as means toward a final break. The pamphlet founded revolutionary Marxism's case against gradual change alone. No public domain English translation exists, so the German text stands. Its force shaped socialist debate for decades.
lyfe-joseph-armathy-de-worde:
The Lyfe of Joseph of Armathy is a prose saint's life from the early days of English printing. Wynkyn de Worde, one of London's first printers, issued the original. This text is an 1871 reprint of that Tudor book, spelling and all.

Joseph of Arimathea stands here as the apostle of Britain, the man who brought the faith to the island. The life tells of his travels, his preaching, and the holy blood he guarded. Such books fed the devotion of ordinary readers in Tudor England. Behind the Grail romances stands this plainer, pious figure, honored as a saint.
martin-hyde:
John Masefield published Martin Hyde in 1910. An older Hyde looks back on his wild youth in its pages. As a teen he served the Duke of Monmouth in 1685.

Monmouth rose against King James II, and his bid for the throne failed. Young Hyde tells of leaving home, going to sea, and meeting friends and foes. Sea scenes, night sounds, and the road to Lyme fill the early part of the tale. The 2011 reprint used here keeps the full chapter list intact. Storm, sherbet, and brave deeds at sea fill its later heads.
menger-grundsaetze-1871-de:
Carl Menger published Grundsätze der Volkswirtschaftslehre in 1871, in German. No public-domain English translation exists, so the text stands here in German. Menger, a Viennese economist, wrote the Principles of Economics as the first part of a larger planned work that never appeared.

Menger grounded value in human needs: a good is worth what the least urgent want it satisfies is worth. From that idea of marginal utility he built accounts of price, trade, and the origin of money. The book founded the Austrian school of economics. Its method, starting from the single choosing person, later set Austrians against both German historicists and, in part, the mainstream of the field.
nasa-tm-19660008277-the-lewis-proton-shi:
R I Hildebrand and H E Renkel at Lewis Research Center described a computer code that calculates radiation dose behind shields, in this 1966 memorandum. The code is written in Fortran IV. It handles shields made of many layers of material. Protons arrive from space as the primary radiation. Collisions inside the shield then create secondary protons and neutrons.

The code computes the particle spectra and the dose behind the layers. Crews and electronics both need that dose kept low. Testing every shield design in the lab would take years. A trusted code let designers compare many shields quickly, and pick the lightest one that still protected well.
nasa-tm-19660009082-study-of-co-radicals:
Jack H Lunsford and John P Jayne at Lewis Research Center used a sensitive magnetic method to study carbon monoxide on a white powder, in a March 1965 article draft. The powder is magnesium oxide, a common catalyst support. The method is electron paramagnetic resonance, which detects certain unpaired electrons. It can reveal radicals, short-lived fragments of molecules, sitting on a surface.

The authors report that about five percent of the carbon monoxide gas took part in the effect they studied. The spectrum, adsorption, and bonding of the radicals are their subjects. Surface chemistry like this underlies catalysts used across industry. Their work shows a space agency laboratory probing basic questions with delicate tools.
nasa-tm-19660015637-use-of-the-adsorptio:
Kenneth O Sizemore, in Goddard's Spacecraft Technology Division, studied special electrodes inside nickel-cadmium cells in April 1966. Spacecraft batteries of that type can build up gas as they charge and discharge. An adsorption hydrogen electrode and an oxygen fuel-cell electrode can consume those gases inside the cell. Sizemore reports the traits and the use of both electrodes.

Gas pressure inside a sealed cell can swell or ruin it. Eating the gas as fast as it forms keeps the cell safe. That trick extends battery life on long missions, where no repair is possible. Sizemore's study gave battery designers measured grounds for adding such electrodes to flight cells.
nasa-tm-19680002181-the-effects-of-ammon:
Frank W. Gilleland, at the Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, exposed solar cells to spacecraft gases in October 1967. The cells are silicon, with titanium silver grids and contacts. Proposed attitude control systems could bathe them in ammonium hydrogen sulfide or Freon 14 gas.

Gilleland measured the cells' electrical output and physical condition after exposure. The sulfide atmospheres ranged from below freezing to about room temperature. Freon 14 gas was tested as well. No short-term harm to arrays using such cells is to be expected, he reports. The result cleared those control gases for use near solar arrays.
nasa-tm-19680020414-nac-neutron-activati:
Suzanne T. Weinstein of Lewis Research Center documents a computer code called NAC in this 1968 memorandum. NAC predicts the gamma ray radioactivity that neutrons induce in many kinds of composite materials. Engineers need such forecasts before irradiating materials in reactors or test facilities.

NAC grew out of an earlier code called NAP, with output reshaped for experimenters. Its output lists input data and every reaction for each element in the material. It also gives end-of-irradiation disintegration rates for each reaction. A product isotope inventory adds dose rates at one meter from an unshielded point source. Cyclic irradiation effects can also be calculated.
nasa-tm-19690029250-energy-dependence-of:
Kaichi Maeda wrote this September 1969 Goddard paper, numbered X-641-69-426, on horizontally incident atmospheric muons. Muons are born when cosmic rays strike the upper air. Those arriving horizontally cross one of the longest air paths possible, so the atmosphere filters their energies more than any other arrivals.

Standard diffusion equations cannot treat those slanting paths well, Maeda states. He therefore modifies the Chapman function, a classic air-mass formula, for an atmosphere whose temperature varies with height. Calculations run for both a simple uniform-temperature air model and the standard atmosphere. He also applies them at mountain altitude, naming the laboratory on Mount Chacaltaya in Bolivia. Numerical results and a discussion close the paper.
nasa-tm-19700019391-stability-relations-:
Bevan M. French of the Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this report in March 1970 on siderite, an iron carbonate mineral. It maps where siderite stays stable and where it breaks down. The tests ran in controlled carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide atmospheres, with oxygen levels held by solid buffer mixtures.

For the runs, French first made siderite by heating ferrous oxalate in sealed tubes under high pressure. He then traced the mineral's stability field across temperature, pressure, and oxygen levels. That field proved to be a narrow wedge, edged by breakdown into hematite or magnetite plus gas. Paths leading to plain iron or to wustite, an iron oxide, are not stable ones.
nasa-tm-19710017455-absolute-stability-a:
S M Seltzer of the Marshall Space Flight Center and D D Siljak of the University of Santa Clara wrote this paper on April 2, 1971. It gives a method for proving absolute stability in attitude control systems for large boosters. Attitude control keeps a rocket pointed the right way. For huge launch vehicles, a proof of stability matters more than trial and error.

The authors showed that absolute stability for these systems holds only within limits. They computed the stable regions with a quadratic Liapunov function. That choice also revealed how fast the system settles back after a push. A sample system model illustrates the method. The work served guidance design for the big rockets of the era.
on-the-blockade: Oliver Optic wrote this Civil War sea novel for boys. It belongs to his Blue and the Gray series afloat. The hosted sample preserves only the publisher's series list. That list names companion volumes such as Taken by the Enemy. It also lists the land series, Brother Against Brother. Readers can confirm the author, series, and publisher from the sample. The sample gives no readable text of the novel itself.
podcast-dannyjones-J5bu0G5-uDE:
Nathan Crock, a philosopher, joins Danny Jones in an early episode of the podcast, recorded when it was still called KONCRETE, for a lesson in philosophical reasoning: how to argue. Crock explains the structure of good arguments, the fallacies that break them, and how to tell a real disagreement from a performance.

The episode is a toolbox disguised as a conversation. Jones supplies the examples and objections, and Crock rebuilds them properly. Listeners who have sat through this series' parades of extraordinary claims will find the standards here quietly devastating, or quietly useful, depending on their loyalties. Few entries in the collection teach a skill outright. This one does, and its skill is the one every other episode in the archive demands of its audience: reasoning well about claims that reason alone struggles to hold.
queen-hildegarde: Queen Hildegarde is a book by Laura E. Richards, but the pages shown here are a publisher's catalogue of her works rather than the story itself. The lists give prices for Star Bright and Captain January. They price the Stories for Little Folks sets too. Five Minute Stories and Three Minute Stories are among them. The Captain January series is listed. Further titles stand at ninety cents. A heading for the Hildegarde-Margaret series begins at the foot of the page.
rhymes-a-la-mode:
A. Lang published these light verses with Kegan Paul, Trench of London in 1885, the year given in Roman figures on the title page. A note says many pieces had run in English or American periodicals, and some in an American set called Ballades and Verses Vain. None had before appeared in book form in England.

A dedicatory ballade leads, then The Fortunate Islands, The New Millennium, and Almae Matres. The titled section holds ballades of middle age, summer, and Christmas ghosts. Love's Easter, a Ballade of the Girton Girl, Ronsard's Grave, and San Terenzo show Lang's range: school, love, travel, and old French forms worn lightly.
rilla-of-ingleside:
Lucy Maud Montgomery tells the war years through Rilla of Ingleside in thirty-five chapters of contents. Glen Notes and Other Matters opens the book, and The Piper Pipes and The Sound of a Going sound the call to war early. Susan, Rilla, and Dog Monday Make a Resolution stands as a chapter of its own.

A War-Baby and a Soup Tureen joins the war to home life, and Rilla Decides follows. Later titles darken: In the Days of Langemarck, They Shall Not Pass, Black Sunday, and Wounded and Missing. A war-wedding, word from Jem, and Victory carry the list toward its close, Rilla-My-Rilla, with Dog Monday knowing more than most.
selected-poems-of-oscar-wilde:
Methuen issued this choice of Oscar Wilde's poems in London in 1911, drawing on the fuller collected edition of 1908 and 1909. The volume holds The Ballad of Reading Gaol as its centerpiece. Wilde's poems had first come out in book form in 1881 and sold through four printings by the end of 1882.

Title pages here trace the Ballad's own strange path in print. Leonard Smithers first issued it in 1898 under the cell mark C. 3. 3., with no name attached. Wilde's name reached the title page only with the seventh edition. Readers get fine poems plus a small history of how they reached print.
selected-prose-of-oscar-wilde:
Methuen issued this choice of Oscar Wilde's prose in 1914, with a preface by Robert Ross. The contents mix short essays, fancies, and brief scenes in Wilde's sharp, playful manner. Titles range from pieces on George Meredith and Robert Browning to whims on climate and art.

Short items carry names like Life the Disciple, Life the Plagiarist, and The Indispensable East. Longer pieces treat Thomas Griffiths Wainewright and Cardinal Newman. A letter and a rejected prize essay close the list. Readers meet Wilde the critic and wit at his most nimble, turning small topics into bright talk.
simmel-philosophie-des-geldes-1900-de:
Georg Simmel published Philosophie des Geldes in 1900, in German. No public-domain English translation exists, so the text stands here in German. Simmel, a Berlin philosopher and early sociologist, asked what money does to the whole of modern life, far beyond buying and selling.

Money, he argued, turns quality into quantity and frees persons from old bonds while chilling their ties. It widens freedom, trade, and choice, yet flattens taste and trust into price. Simmel ranged from art and love to cities and strangers in one flowing analysis. The book is a founding work on the culture of money, read beside Marx and Weber by students of modern society.
the-amazing-interlude:
Mary Roberts Rinehart's 1918 war novel, pictured by the Kinneys, starts with a stage figure: most lives, it says, play out on one fixed set. Sara Lee Kennedy seems set for just such a steady life, with no change of scene ahead of her.

Then the backdrop turns clear and a strange new scene shows through. Picture captions name an officer named Henri and speak of Belgians who might one day go home again. War in Europe breaks Sara Lee's calm routine, and her small drama is pulled onto a far larger stage of loss, aid work, and love under fire.
the-bride:
Samuel Rowlands wrote The Bride, a poem entered in the Stationers' Register on May 22, 1617. A first note by Alfred Claghorn Potter tells its strange past. When Rowlands's complete works came out from the Hunterian Club between 1872 and 1880, the editor had to leave this poem out. No copy was thought to survive. Twenty years later the Dictionary of National Biography still listed it as lost.

Last spring, the note says, a copy turned up in the catalogue of a bookseller in a small German town. It was bought for the Harvard College Library from the Child Memorial Fund. The copy is whole but for torn inner corners on the second and third leaves, with parts of two words lost and supplied by hand. This reprint is made from that copy, page for page and word for word.
the-englishing-of-french-words-the-diale:
The Englishing of French Words, by Brander Matthews, shares S.P.E. Tract number five, printed at the Clarendon Press in 1921, with Robert Bridges on the dialect words in Blunden's poems. Matthews likens the English tongue to an inn of strange meetings: words of blue blood rub with gutter-born strays, and sea terms from Scandinavia sit by war words from France.

Some guests tarry and leave; some settle and found lines that match the oldest stock. Matthews traces how French words took English form. The tract suits readers who love the mixed blood of English speech.
the-eureka-stockade: The Eureka Stockade, by Raffaello Carboni, is the work named across the old Project Gutenberg header pages at the front of this text. Those pages give the title and author, amid long notes on copyright and gifts to the project. Only the header matter is present here. None of Carboni's narrative appears, beyond his name and theme: the gold miners' armed stand at Ballarat.
the-fur-country-or-seventy-degrees-north:
Jules Verne wrote The Fur Country, a tale of the far north first printed in French in 1873 and turned into English by N. D'Anvers. The translator gives the work to her three nephews.

The head note sorts this tale as the tenth in the standard list of Verne's works and names later English versions. Verne sends a Hudson's Bay party to found a fort at seventy degrees north, on land that proves to be ice. A quake, a drift, and a long float on a melting island turn a trade post into a fight to live, led by a calm officer and a brave woman guest.
the-gay-cockade: Temple Bailey wrote The Gay Cockade as a set of tales, printed under a copyright of 1921. The front matter thanks the editors of many magazines. The tales first ran in Harper's, Scribner's, Collier's, and other such journals. Only the front matter is present here. It ends as the contents list begins. Bailey's past books named on the title page include The Trumpeter Swan and The Tin Soldier. No tale text can be read in this opening portion. So the stories cannot be described from the front matter alone.
the-good-comrade: Una L. Silberrad wrote The Good Comrade. Doubleday, Page and Company printed it in New York in 1907. Pictures are by Anna Whelan Betts. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page and a contents list. The heads open with The Polkingtons and The Debt. They turn to a flower, Narcissus Triandrus Azureum. They name The Owner of the Blue Daffodil. Later heads name Pooferchjes and Jealousy, The Holiday, and A Reprieve. A debt and a rare blue daffodil seem to drive the plot.
the-lady-of-lyons-or-love-and-pride:
Edward Bulwer Lytton inscribed this play to the author of Ion. That author's genius had helped revive the national drama, he says. His preface explains the plot's source. A faint memory of a tale called The Bellows-Mender suggested it. The incidents were greatly altered. The characters were entirely recast. He chose the French Republic's era deliberately. Its ferment and brief leveling of ranks suited his design. Claude's high-placed love and rapid career became probable there.

The play also served the stage itself. Lytton wrote partly to support Macready's management at Covent Garden. He also tested whether critics were right about his gift. The Duchess de la Valliere had failed by comparison. They said his gift was not dramatic. The result tells of a peasant posing as a prince. He wins Pauline that way. The play became a much-revived melodrama.
the-life-of-froude:
Herbert Paul published his life of the historian James Anthony Froude with Pitman in London in 1905. Chapter one skips genealogy by design. Paul says a man himself, not his ancestors, deserves a written life, and Froude held the same view.

Froude was born at Dartington in Devon on April 23, 1818, St George Day and Shakespeare birthday. His clergyman father took a pass degree at Oxford before taking orders. Paul sketches a yeoman family settled in Devon for ages, then moves toward the boy who became a bold, disputed voice in Victorian history writing.
the-missing-bride:
Mrs. E. D. E. N. Southworth's novel The Missing Bride opens at Luckenough, an ancient manor house deep in the forest of St. Mary's. The house stands between the Patuxent and Wicomico Rivers in Maryland. Southworth's earlier novels, including Ishmael, Self-Raised, and Retribution, are listed on the title page.

Chapter I tells the manor's founding legend. Alexander Kalouga, a Polish soldier of fortune, was said to have been born in one quarter of the globe, schooled in another, and blooded in a third. Local tradition made him a pupil of Guy Fawkes who escaped after the Gunpowder Plot, then a buccaneer in Spanish America and a hired sword across Europe. Leonard Calvert brought him to Maryland, where the Lord Proprietary granted him the manor.
the-morris-book-part-1-a-history-of-morr:
Front matter only is present here for Part I of The Morris Book, by Cecil J. Sharp and Herbert C. Macilwaine, published in London by Novello and Company in 1907, so the dance descriptions do not appear. The full title promises a history of morris dancing with descriptions of eleven dances as performed by the morris-men of England. A frontispiece shows morris dancers from an old stained-glass window at Betley, Staffordshire.

The book was issued alongside the authors' Morris Dance Tunes and dedicated to their friends and pupils, the members of the Esperance Girls' Club at Cumberland Market. A short preface of thanks names Lady Isabel Margesson, Florence Warren, and the Rev. S. Baring Gould, who allowed use of an old woodcut of Kemp, the man who danced from London to Norwich.
the-nursery-number-164-a-monthly-magazin: Number 164 of The Nursery came out in August 1880, in volume XXVII of the Boston monthly for the youngest readers, at $1.50 a year. Only the front matter and contents are present here, so the stories and poems themselves do not appear. The number opens with The Little Teacher by Dora Burnside and The Ant's Dairy. It also lists The Friendly Dog by Uncle Charles, Charley Goes A-Fishing, and What We Saw in the Woods.
the-poetical-works-of-mark-akenside:
The Poetical Works of Mark Akenside, edited by the Reverend George Gilfillan, opens with a life of the poet. Akenside was born at Newcastle-upon-Tyne on November 9, 1721, into a family of Presbyterian Dissenters. He was baptized at the end of that month in the Hanover Square meeting by Benjamin Bennet. His father, also Mark, was a butcher of respectable standing. His mother was Mary Lumsden.

Gilfillan finds nothing anti-poetical in a butcher's shop as a birthplace for the author of The Pleasures of Imagination. Henry Kirke White was likewise a butcher's son, and Cardinal Wolsey's case is famous. Akenside, it is said, was ashamed of his origin. Gilfillan treats his lifelong lameness, begun by a cut from his father's cleaver, as a fitting reminder of that smallness. The boy's schooling and rise into medicine and poetry follow in the life.
the-prince-and-the-page-a-story-of-the-l:
The Prince and the Page, a story of the last crusade, was written by the author of The Heir of Redclyffe and printed by Macmillan in London in a 1909 reprint. Adrian Stokes drew the frontispiece. The title page carries a long publishing history: first edition in 1865, then reprint after reprint through 1909, with a shilling edition in 1908. Few children's books of its day can have been reissued so often.

A preface opens by saying that in these days of exactness even a child's historical romance must point to its proofs. The author's, she admits, do not lie very deep. She names the picture of Simon de Montfort drawn from his wife's household books, as quoted in Mrs. Everett Green's Lives of the Princesses. Edward I in Carte's History stands beside it. The honesty of that opening sets the terms for the tale of crusading times that follows.
the-quaker-colonies-a-chronicle-of-the-p:
Sydney G. Fisher recounts the Delaware proprietors in a 1919 volume. Yale University Press issued it in the Chronicles of America series. Chapter one begins in 1661. Seventeen-year-old William Penn is then a student at Christ Church, Oxford. His father is an admiral in favor at the restored court. Charles the Second has just regained the throne.

Thirteen chapters carry the story through Penn's voyage and early Philadelphia life. They cover troubles with his sons and the French and Indian War. They end with the decline of Quaker government. The account then turns to New Jersey and to Delaware. A bibliography closes the volume. Students of colonial America get a compact political history. It centers on Penn's experiment in government.
the-silver-horde: Rex Beach's The Silver Horde is represented here by a list of his books and the start of a contents list. No chapter text follows. Beach also wrote The Spoilers, The Iron Trail, and The Auction Block, the list says. The contents uses a running formula of wherein and in which. A spiritless man and a rogue appear first. They break bread with a lonely woman next. Cherry Malotte displays a temper, then gives heart to a hopeless man.
the-star-of-gettysburg-a-story-of-southe: Joseph A. Altsheler wrote this story of southern high tide as a full romance. It belongs to his Civil War series. The series runs from The Guns of Bull Run onward. It passes The Sword of Antietam before this volume. The pages here hold a short foreword. It explains that arrangement. A series list and a roster of principal characters follow. Harry Kenton heads the roster. He is a lad fighting on the southern side. His cousin Dick Mason fights for the north. The Gettysburg story itself does not appear.
the-sunny-side:
A. A. Milne gathered these humorous pieces in 1922, dedicating the book affectionately to Owen Seaman in memory of nine happy years at the Punch office. A contents list divides the sketches under oranges and lemons, men of letters, summer days, war-time, home notes, a few guests, and others, and the first section opens with an invitation.

Simpson writes to Myra at the beginning of the year that he has an important suggestion to make to them both, and is coming round tomorrow night after dinner about nine. Dahlia and Archie are asked to meet him there. If the household has gone out, the visitors will simply wait. They will wait until it comes back. The start is pure Milne. A social trifle promises outsized comedy.
the-tables-turned-or-nupkins-awakened-a-: William Morris wrote this socialist interlude for the Hall of the Socialist League. He also wrote The Earthly Paradise. The play was first performed on Saturday, October 15, 1887. It was printed that year at the office of The Commonweal in London. Only the title page and part one's original cast list appear here, naming Mr. La-di-da, found guilty of swindling, Mr. Justice Nupkins, Mary Pinch played by May Morris, Jack Freeman, and the Archbishop of Canterbury played by Morris himself, so the play itself does not appear.
the-trail-horde: Charles Alden Seltzer's Trail Horde was published by A. C. McClurg of Chicago in September 1920, with a frontispiece by P. V. E. Ivory. This record holds the title page and contents, ending partway through the chapter list. Headings move from Concerning Morals and Driving a Bargain through the invisible power, a coalition, the long trail, Lawler's nerve, and a line cabin in a storm. A caption shows a gunman warning Warden that a quarter-inch move means death. Seltzer's fight is mapped, but his first chapter is not here.
the-trees-of-pride:
G. K. Chesterton's Trees of Pride is built in four parts, from The Tale of the Peacock Trees to The Chase after the Truth. It opens on Squire Vane, an Irish-bred, English-schooled squire whose education left his intellect permanently boyish. His bodily impatience made him a radiant failure in diplomatic service. Sent to meet Muslims halfway, he kicked off one boot at a mosque gate, an aggressive indifference mistaken on all sides.

Vane prides himself on plain sense, yet forever does nonsensical things, standing on his head to prove he is hard-headed. Breakfasting outdoors by the Cornish coast with his grave, red-haired daughter Barbara, he is about to wager on the legend of the peacock trees. Chesterton sets a detective fable among rationalists and legends.
the-young-woman-s-guide:
William A. Alcott's The Young Woman's Guide followed his Young Man's Guide, his preface explains. Publication was deferred while companion volumes appeared first. Alcott warns that he offers no complete manual of women's duties. Some duties, he felt, received too little attention from other writers. Temperance in all things concerns him especially. His own viewpoint, he admits freely, shapes the selections.

Alcott wrote many such guides on health and conduct. Young women of his era were their intended readers. Duties he judged neglected get fuller treatment here. Relative duties within family and society structure the advice. Readers today can study it as evidence of nineteenth-century expectations placed on young women.
tonnies-gemeinschaft-gesellschaft-1887-d:
Ferdinand Tönnies published Gemeinschaft und Gesellschaft in 1887, in German, in its first edition. No public-domain English translation exists, so the text stands here in German. Tönnies, a young German scholar, drew a line between two kinds of human bond that sociology still uses.

Gemeinschaft, or community, names the warm ties of family, village, and custom, held by feeling and habit. Gesellschaft, or society, names the cold ties of trade, cities, and contract, held by calculation. Modern life, he argued, shifts from the first toward the second. That simple pair became a founding tool of sociology, used to describe everything from rural loss to modern loneliness.
verner-s-pride: Mrs. Henry Wood wrote Verner's Pride. Collins' Clear-Type Press issued it, with pictures by Harold Piffard. Pages shown here hold the title page and a contents list, so the novel itself is not shown. Early chapters name Rachel Frost, a willow pond, and news brought home. A crowd in the moonlight, a tall gentleman in a lane, and a ghost tale follow. One chapter promises a revelation at an inquest. Later titles name a night before a wedding, a troubled mind, and an altered will.
via-crucis-a-romance-of-the-second-crusa:
F. Marion Crawford wrote Via Crucis, a romance of the Second Crusade. Its picture list promises the knighting of Gilbert, Gilbert with Beatrix, and crowds crying for crosses. Chapter one opens at sunset on the fifth day of May, in the year 1145. The scene is the garden of Stoke Regis Manor. A lady walks a narrow path between high rose bushes trained on the manor wall.

Crawford lingers on the scene. Spiked rushes grow at the water's edge, and close-cropped grass runs beyond it. Great oaks stand in spring leaf, and corn land rolls to the horizon. The low sun reddens the lady's golden hair and fires her clear blue eyes. Within a year, the preaching of the cross will pull men like Gilbert from such quiet gardens to war in the East. Readers get a polished historical romance rooted in an English spring.
voyage-of-the-liberdade: Captain Joshua Slocum wrote Voyage of the Liberdade, issued at Boston in 1890. Pages present here hold a contents list whose chapter notes sketch the whole cruise, so the narrative itself is not shown. The notes promise a ship, a crew, and a hurricane. The Cape Verde Islands, Montevideo, and the salvage of a wine cargo follow. Cholera in the Argentine and hard quarantine at Ilha Grande come next. Rio at last, and storms called pampeiros that lay the ship on her beam ends, close the list.
weymouth-new-testament-in-modern-speech-:
Jude is book 65 in R. F. Weymouth's modern speech New Testament, third edition, 1913. Jude calls himself a servant of Christ and a brother of James. He writes to those held in God's love and kept for Christ. He had meant to write on shared salvation, he says, but a sharper need came up.

False men have slipped in without being seen. They twist grace into an excuse for wrong and deny Christ as Lord. Jude recalls Egypt, fallen angels, and Sodom as warnings from the past. Michael the archangel even disputed with the Devil over Moses' body. Weymouth's version makes the fierce little letter plain to follow.
wilfrid-cumbermede: Only the title page and contents are present here for George MacDonald's Wilfrid Cumbermede, so the novel itself does not appear. F. A. Fraser drew fourteen full-page pictures. The contents open with an introduction, then Wilfrid finding himself and meeting his uncle and aunt. A sword on the wall, lessons, cobbling, and school fill the early chapters. Later titles name a ghost, an ice-cave, mountains, and a frozen stream. Charley nurses Wilfrid, then goes to Oxford in the list. A white mare and London close it.
you-never-know-your-luck-being-the-story:
Gilbert Parker wrote this prairie novel about a matrimonial deserter in the town of Askatoon. Pages present here hold a full contents list for three volumes and the start of an introduction. Parker explains that companion novels share this western setting and cast. The World for Sale and The Money Master treat the same prairie people. Some figures also move through Wild Youth.

The contents promise a proem, a trial at Logan, and a story told by the deserter himself. Later parts cover an unopened letter and a final verdict. Readers get Parker's map of his prairie cycle before the tale starts. Desertion and its fallout drive the plot.
